title: OSI & TCP/IP
subtitle: Follow the jobs that turn application data into signals.

nodes.title: 1 · Physical
nodes.definition: The physical layer provides movement of individual bits from one hop to the next.
nodes.example: A cable carries bits as signals.

nodes.title: 2 · Data Link
nodes.definition: Data Link provides hop-to-hop frame delivery.
nodes.example: An Ethernet frame crosses one local link.

nodes.title: 3 · Network
nodes.definition: The network layer handles logical addresses and source-to-destination packet delivery.
nodes.example: A router sends an IP packet toward another network.

nodes.title: 4 · Transport
nodes.definition: Transport provides process-to-process delivery, using port addresses.
nodes.example: Port numbers distinguish the applications communicating.

nodes.title: 5 · Session
nodes.definition: Synchronization with checkpoints is a session-layer function.
nodes.example: A checkpoint helps a transfer resume.

nodes.title: 6 · Presentation
nodes.definition: These are the functions listed for the presentation layer.
nodes.example: Text can be translated into another representation.

nodes.title: 7 · Application
nodes.definition: Provides network services for applications, such as web access and mail.
nodes.example: HTTP exchanges web requests and responses.
nodes.compare: It provides networking services; it is not the entire browser program.

nodes.title: TCP/IP model
nodes.definition: The original TCP/IP suite has four layers; the notes also show a five-layer comparison with OSI.
nodes.example: Group the OSI upper layers into the TCP/IP application layer.
nodes.compare: The notes describe both the original four-layer model and the five-layer teaching comparison.

nodes.title: Encapsulation
nodes.definition: Encapsulation adds each layer's information before passing data to the next lower layer.
nodes.example: Application data → segment → packet → frame → bits.
nodes.compare: Decapsulation removes the added information at the receiving side.

title: Network devices
subtitle: Compare what each device sees and forwards.

nodes.title: Repeater · Layer 1
nodes.definition: Regenerates incoming signals to extend a link.
nodes.example: Extend the reach of a LAN signal.
nodes.compare: It does not choose a route or read MAC addresses.

nodes.title: Hub · Layer 1
nodes.definition: Repeats an incoming signal to its other interfaces.
nodes.example: Traffic entering one port is repeated to the other ports.
nodes.compare: A hub does not learn MAC addresses or filter frames.

nodes.title: Switch · Layer 2
nodes.definition: A hub repeats signals, while a switch can forward frames selectively using MAC addresses.
nodes.example: A learned destination MAC address tells the switch which port to use.
nodes.compare: Hub: repeats signals. Basic Ethernet switch: forwards frames using MAC addresses.

nodes.title: Router · Layer 3
nodes.definition: Forwards IP packets between networks using destination IP addresses and routing information.
nodes.example: Connect an office LAN to another IP network.
nodes.compare: Switch: delivery inside a LAN. Router: delivery between IP networks.

nodes.title: How a switch learns
nodes.definition: An Ethernet switch is a Layer 2 device that uses a MAC address table.
nodes.example: The switch records the source MAC address and incoming port.
nodes.compare: An unknown destination is flooded within the same broadcast domain; known unicast can use a specific port.

title: Addresses & delivery
subtitle: Separate the host address, local delivery address and route.

nodes.title: MAC address
nodes.definition: An Ethernet physical address contains 6 bytes, or 48 bits.
nodes.example: 00:1B:21:2E:4F:6A is an Ethernet MAC address.
nodes.compare: MAC is used for local frame delivery; IP is used for routed packet delivery.

nodes.title: IP address
nodes.definition: A logical address used for host-to-host packet delivery across networks.
nodes.example: A packet keeps the remote host as its destination IP when crossing a router without NAT.
nodes.compare: The next-hop MAC address and final destination IP have different jobs.

nodes.title: Subnet mask
nodes.definition: The subnet mask identifies which address bits belong to the network and which to the host.
nodes.compare: The prefix identifies the network part, not the application.

nodes.title: Default route
nodes.definition: The default route represents destinations without another more specific route match.
nodes.example: Use a default route when no more specific route matches.

nodes.title: ARP
nodes.definition: An ARP table stores IP/MAC address mappings for LAN nodes, with a lifetime.
nodes.example: Find the MAC address of the next-hop IPv4 device on the local LAN.
nodes.compare: For a remote destination, resolve the gateway’s MAC address, not the remote host’s.

nodes.title: NAT
nodes.definition: The router replaces the private source IP/port pair with its public IP and a translated port.
nodes.example: Several private hosts can share a public address using port translation.
nodes.compare: Translation changes addresses or ports; it is different from deciding a route.

title: TCP, UDP & services
subtitle: Connect transport behavior to the services applications use.

nodes.title: TCP
nodes.definition: Provides reliable, ordered delivery of a byte stream, using acknowledgments and retransmissions.
nodes.example: A sender retransmits data that was not acknowledged.
nodes.compare: Reliability and ordering are provided by TCP; UDP does not provide them by itself.

nodes.title: TCP handshake
nodes.definition: TCP uses a three-way handshake to agree on a connection and initial sequence numbers.
nodes.example: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK before normal data exchange.

nodes.title: UDP
nodes.definition: UDP handles segments independently and performs no connection establishment.
nodes.example: An application can send a datagram without a TCP-style connection setup.
nodes.compare: The application must handle any reliability it needs.

nodes.title: Ports & connections
nodes.definition: TCP uses a four-tuple to distinguish simultaneous connections.
nodes.example: Two connections to the same server can have different source ports.
nodes.compare: IP identifies a host interface; a port helps identify an application endpoint.

nodes.title: DNS
nodes.definition: DNS is a distributed application-layer service for name/address translation.
nodes.example: Resolve a website name to an IP address.
nodes.compare: DNS resolves names; DHCP supplies network configuration.

nodes.title: DHCP
nodes.definition: Automatically supplies IPv4 network settings, including an address, mask and gateway.
nodes.example: Discover → Offer → Request → Acknowledge (DORA).
nodes.compare: DHCP configures the client; DNS helps it find addresses for names.
